source.title: International first aid, resuscitation and education guidelines 2020
source.publisher: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC)
source.terms: The IFRC allows copies of all or part of the guidelines for non-commercial use, providing the source is acknowledged.

meta.scope_note: For teenagers and adults. Babies and young children need different steps: tell the 112 operator the age.
meta.left_out: Medicine doses are left out on purpose (for example aspirin for chest pain). Ask the 112 operator.

guides.chat_now: Call {number} now, or ask someone to call. Shout and tap their shoulders. If they don't respond, look and listen: are they breathing normally? If not, start CPR: open the guide below.
guides.title: Someone collapsed: start here
guides.when: You are not sure what is wrong.

steps.text: Make sure the place is safe for you, for example from traffic, fire or electricity. Go to the person only when it is safe.
Shout their name and tap their shoulders. Do they respond?
Look at their chest and listen. Are they breathing normally? Gasping, noisy or very slow breathing is NOT normal.

notes: If you are not sure whether they are breathing normally, start CPR. That is what the Red Cross guidelines advise.

guides.title: Not responding and not breathing normally
guides.when: No response to voice or touch, and no breathing or only gasping.

steps.text: Call {number} now, or ask someone nearby to call. Put the phone on speaker so your hands are free.
steps.log: Called or asked someone to call {number}

steps.text: Kneel beside them. Put the heel of one hand in the middle of the chest, the other hand on top, fingers locked together.
With straight arms, push hard, straight down, about 5 cm, then let the chest come all the way back up. Push on every beat: 100 to 120 times a minute.
Keep going without stopping until help takes over, or they cough, open their eyes, move on purpose or breathe normally.

do_not: Do not stop to look for a pulse. A pulse check is unreliable and wastes time.
Do not stop compressions to wait for the ambulance.
notes: If a defibrillator (AED) is nearby, ask someone to bring it, switch it on and follow its voice.
If someone else can take over, swap so you don't get too tired, with as little pause as possible.
If you are carrying the person to hospital, keep CPR going on a firm surface.

guides.title: Not responding but breathing normally
guides.when: No response to voice or touch, but normal, regular breathing.

steps.text: Roll them onto their side and gently tilt their head back. This keeps the airway open and stops them choking if they vomit.
steps.log: Put on their side, airway open

steps.text: Call {number}. Someone who does not respond needs help, even if they breathe.
Stay with them and keep checking their breathing. If they stop breathing normally, start CPR.

do_not: If you think they hurt their neck or back, do not roll them. Keep the airway open by tilting the head and lifting the chin.

guides.chat_now: Act now: if they cannot cough or speak, give up to 5 sharp blows between the shoulder blades, then up to 5 abdominal thrusts, and keep repeating. Ask someone to call {number}. The guide below shows each step.
guides.title: Choking
guides.when: Something is stuck in the throat.

steps.text: Can they cough, speak or breathe?
Tell them to keep coughing. Stay with them and watch closely: it can get worse.
Stand behind them, bend them forward, and give up to 5 sharp blows between the shoulder blades with the heel of your hand.
Still blocked? Stand behind, put a fist between the belly button and the ribs, hold it with your other hand, and pull sharply in and up, up to 5 times.
Still blocked? Call {number} now. Keep repeating 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts.

do_not: Do not sweep inside the mouth blindly with your fingers: it can push the object further down. Only take out something you can see.
notes: Babies under one year need different steps. Tell the 112 operator the age.

guides.chat_now: Press hard on the wound with a cloth and keep pressing. Call {number}, or ask someone to call while you press. Help them lie down.
guides.title: Heavy bleeding
guides.when: Blood is flowing fast from a wound.

steps.text: Press hard on the wound. Use a cloth, bandage or plastic between your hand and the blood. If they can, they can press it themselves.
Help them lie down, so they do not faint and fall.
Call {number}, or ask someone to call while you keep pressing.
If blood soaks through, put another cloth on top and press harder. Do not lift the first cloth.
steps.log: Added a second cloth, pressed harder

steps.text: Only if pressing does not stop heavy bleeding from an arm or leg, and you have a tourniquet: put it on above the wound. The time is saved for the doctor.
Keep them lying down and warm, for example covered with clothes or a blanket.

do_not: If an object such as a knife is stuck in the wound, do not pull it out. Press around it.

guides.chat_now: Call {number} now. Help them sit down and rest, and keep them calm. Ask someone to bring a defibrillator (AED) if there is one nearby.
guides.title: Chest pain
guides.when: Pain or pressure in the chest that does not go away.

steps.text: Help them sit down in a comfortable position. If a doctor prescribed them heart medicine for this, help them take it.
steps.log: Sitting down, helped with own medicine if any

steps.text: Call {number} now. Ask someone to bring a defibrillator (AED) if there is one nearby.
Stay with them, keep them calm, and watch their breathing and whether they respond. If they stop responding and are not breathing normally, start CPR.

notes: Women, older people and people with diabetes may have milder or unusual signs. If in doubt, treat it as serious.
Medicine doses are not given here. Ask the 112 operator what to give.

links.label: They stopped responding or breathing normally

guides.chat_now: Call {number} now: these can be signs of a stroke. Note the time the signs started. Keep them comfortable and give nothing to eat or drink.
guides.title: Signs of a stroke
guides.when: Sudden weak face or arm, or strange speech.

steps.text: Ask them to smile. Does one side of the face droop?
Ask them to raise both arms. Does one arm drift down or not move?
Ask them to repeat a simple sentence. Is their speech slurred or strange?
Any of these signs? Call {number} now. Tell them when the signs started, or the last time the person was seen well. If you don't know, say so.
Help them into a comfortable position and support them so they don't fall. Keep talking to them and watch their breathing.

do_not: Do not give them anything to eat or drink: swallowing may not be safe.
notes: Even if the signs go away, they still need a doctor quickly.
Very high or low blood sugar can look similar. Tell the doctor about diabetes.

guides.chat_now: Call {number} now. Help them lie down and keep as still as possible. Do not tie the limb, cut the bite or suck out the venom.
guides.title: Snakebite
guides.when: Bitten by a snake, or you think so.

steps.text: Help them lie down and keep as still as possible. Moving makes the venom spread faster.
Call {number}. They need a hospital that has antivenom.
Take off rings, bangles, watches and tight clothes near the bite before it swells. Move the limb as little as possible.
If help is far away, keep the bitten arm or leg still with a cloth or non-stretchy bandage wrapped around it. Do not wrap it tight.
Do not let them walk on a bitten leg. Carry them, for example two people making a chair with their arms.
Keep watching their breathing and whether they respond. If it is safe, take a photo of the snake from a distance.

do_not: Do not tie a tight band (tourniquet) around the limb.
Do not cut the bite or suck out the venom.
Do not put ice on it or rub it.
Do not try to catch or kill the snake.

links.label: They stopped responding or breathing normally

guides.chat_now: Move hard or sharp things away and put something soft under their head. Do not hold them down or put anything in their mouth. Call {number} if it lasts more than 5 minutes, it is their first seizure, or they are hurt.
guides.title: Seizure (fit)
guides.when: Shaking, stiffening or not responding with twitching.

steps.text: Tap Done now: the seizure start time is saved for the doctor.
Move hard or sharp things away. Do not move them unless they are in danger, for example on a road.
Put something soft under their head. Take off glasses and loosen anything tight around the neck.
Call {number} if: it is their first seizure, it lasts more than 5 minutes, they are hurt, they don't wake up after, it happens again, they are pregnant or diabetic, or you are not sure.
When the shaking stops, tap Done: the stop time is saved.
Now check their breathing. Are they breathing normally?

do_not: Do not hold them down.
Do not put anything in their mouth or between their teeth.
Do not give them food, drink or medicine until they are fully awake.

guides.chat_now: If they are awake and can swallow, give something sugary now: their own glucose tablets, fruit juice or a sugary (not diet) drink, or sweets. Help them sit down. Call {number} if they cannot swallow safely, get more drowsy, have a fit or stop responding.
guides.title: Low blood sugar (diabetes)
guides.when: Someone with diabetes is sweating, shaky, weak, confused or drowsy.

steps.text: Are they awake and able to swallow safely?

choices.label: No, very drowsy or not responding

steps.text: Help them sit down.
Give something sugary now: their own glucose tablets if they have them, or a glass of fruit juice or a sugary (not diet) drink, or a few spoonfuls of sugar or some sweets.
Stay with them. If they still feel unwell after 15 minutes, give something sugary again.
Call {number} if they are not clearly better in about 30 minutes, or if they get more drowsy, have a fit or stop responding. Keep watching their breathing.
When they feel better, give them something more filling, such as a slice of bread or a chapati, and check their blood sugar if they have a meter.

do_not: Only give food or drink if they are awake and able to swallow: otherwise it can choke them.
Do not give diet or sugar-free drinks or sweets: they do not raise blood sugar.
notes: If you are not sure whether their sugar is low or high, treat it as low: sugar is unlikely to harm someone whose sugar is high, but not giving it to someone whose sugar is low can.

guides.chat_now: Help them sit up, leaning forward with their arms resting on something, and loosen tight clothes. If they have an inhaler, help them use it. Call {number} now if it does not help within a few minutes or there is none, if they cannot speak, their lips turn blue, or they get confused or sleepy.
guides.title: Breathing difficulty or asthma attack
guides.when: Short of breath, wheezing, or an asthma attack.

steps.text: Help them sit up, leaning forward with their arms resting on a table or on their knees. Stay calm and reassure them.
If they have their own inhaler or medicine for this, help them use it. Loosen tight clothing and move them away from smoke or dust.

Call {number} now if: there is no inhaler and it lasts more than a few minutes, the inhaler does not help within a few minutes, it is very hard to breathe or speak, their lips or fingers turn blue, they get confused or sleepy, or their breathing becomes slow and quieter as they tire.
Stay with them, calm and sitting up, until their breathing is normal. They may use their inhaler again as their doctor prescribed.

do_not: Do not make them lie flat.
notes: Fast breathing from panic (with dizziness or tingling hands): take them somewhere quiet and ask them to breathe slowly into their cupped hands.
If they stop responding, open "Someone collapsed: start here".

guides.chat_now: If the lips, tongue or throat swell, or breathing is hard, call {number} now: it may be a severe allergic reaction. If they have an adrenaline (epinephrine) auto-injector, help them use it in the middle of the outer thigh. Help them lie down, or sit up if breathing is hard.
guides.title: Severe allergic reaction
guides.when: Swelling of the lips, tongue or throat, hives, or trouble breathing after a food, a sting or a medicine.

steps.text: Is it severe: swelling of the lips, tongue or throat, trouble breathing or wheezing, or feeling faint?

choices.label: No, only an itchy rash or sneezing

steps.text: Call {number} now. Say it may be a severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis).
If they have their own adrenaline (epinephrine) auto-injector, help them use it now in the middle of the outer thigh. It can go through thin clothes. Tell the ambulance team when it was given.
Help them lie down. If breathing is hard, help them sit up instead.
steps.log: Lying down, or sitting if breathing is hard

steps.text: Keep watching their breathing and whether they respond. If they are not better 5 to 10 minutes after the injection and have a second one, it may be used.
For a mild reaction: move them away from what caused it, or rinse it off the skin, and help them take their own allergy medicine if they have it. Watch for any of the severe signs.

do_not: Do not wait to see if it gets better when the lips, tongue or throat swell or breathing is hard.
notes: A severe reaction can come back: watch them closely for the next three days.
Someone who has had a severe reaction should always carry an allergy card.

guides.chat_now: Stop more contact with the poison: take it away, or get them into fresh air if it is safe for you. Call {number} and say what it was, how much and when. Do not make them vomit. Keep the bottle or packet.
guides.title: Poisoning
guides.when: Swallowed medicines, a chemical, kerosene, a pesticide or a plant, or breathed in gas or smoke.

steps.text: Stop more contact with the poison. Take it away from them. With gas or smoke, get them into fresh air only if it is safe for you.
steps.log: Stopped more contact with the poison

steps.text: Find out what it was, how much and when. Touch the packet only if it is safe.
steps.log: Found out what, how much and when

steps.text: Call {number} and tell them what it was, how much and when. Follow their instructions.
Help them into a comfortable position, on their left side if possible. Watch their breathing and whether they respond.
steps.log: On their left side, watched breathing

steps.text: Keep the bottles, packets or labels to give to the ambulance team.
steps.log: Kept the packets for the ambulance team

do_not: Do not make them vomit: it can damage the throat.
If they swallowed a strong chemical (such as acid, bleach or drain cleaner), do not give water or milk to dilute it.
notes: Poisoning can look like a fit, a stroke or low blood sugar.
Keep medicines and chemicals locked away and out of reach of children.

guides.chat_now: Cool the burn under clean running water now, for at least 10 minutes and best 20. Take off rings and clothes near it unless they are stuck. Call {number} if the burn is large or deep, on the face, mouth, throat or private parts, or from flames, electricity or a chemical.
guides.title: Burns
guides.when: Burned by fire, hot water, oil, steam, a chemical or electricity.

steps.text: Make it safe first: stop the heat, for example cover a burning pot. With electricity, switch it off before you touch them.
Cool the burn under clean running water for at least 10 minutes, best 20. Let the water flow over it gently. No running water? Use any cool, clean liquid.
steps.log: Cooled the burn with running water

steps.text: Call {number} if the burn is large or deep, on the face, mouth, throat or private parts, or caused by flames, electricity or a chemical. Any burn on a baby, an older person or someone with diabetes needs a doctor.
Take off rings, bangles, watches and clothes on or near the burn, unless they are stuck to the skin.
steps.log: Took off jewellery and clothes near the burn

steps.text: After cooling, cover it loosely with cling film, a clean wet cloth or a non-stick dressing. Cover it, do not wrap it tightly: it may swell.
Keep the rest of the body warm. Watch their breathing and whether they respond, especially for a child or an older person.

do_not: Do not put ice or ice-cold water on a burn.
Do not pop blisters.
Do not pull off clothing that is stuck to the burn.
notes: A chemical on the skin or in the eye: rinse with plenty of clean running water until the pain eases.
If the burn later gets more painful, red and warm, or they get a fever, see a doctor: it may be infected.

guides.chat_now: Ask them to stop and rest, and watch them closely. Call {number} if they were knocked out even for a few seconds, are confused or behaving differently, vomit more than once, have weakness or tingling, double or blurred vision, a bad headache, or blood or clear fluid from the nose or ears.
guides.title: Head injury (fall or blow to the head)

steps.text: Help them stop what they were doing and rest. After a hard fall, keep their head and neck still.

Any of these? Knocked out even for a few seconds; confused, slurred speech or behaving differently; a fit; weakness or tingling in an arm or leg; vomiting more than once; double or blurred vision; blood or clear fluid from the nose or ears; a bad headache for more than 2 hours.
steps.log: Signs of a serious head injury

steps.text: Call {number} now. Keep their head and neck as still as possible: you can hold the head gently with your hands. Keep watching their breathing and whether they respond.
A bump, a mild headache or feeling sick: let them rest and stay with them. Keep watching for the signs above for the next 24 hours, and call {number} if one appears.

do_not: Do not let them drive, use machines or play sport until all signs have gone.
notes: Signs of a serious head injury can appear hours, or even days, later.
After a hard fall or blow, the neck may be hurt too.

guides.chat_now: Help them sit or lie down where they cannot fall. If they lie down, raise their legs. Ask them to cross their legs and squeeze their leg, belly and bottom muscles. If they faint and do not wake up at once, call {number} and check their breathing.
guides.title: Feeling faint or fainting
guides.when: Dizzy, pale, about to faint, or fainted and woke up quickly.

steps.text: Help them sit or lie down on the floor, in a safe place where they cannot fall.
steps.log: Helped them sit or lie down

steps.text: Ask them to cross their legs and squeeze their leg, belly and bottom muscles, or to squat. If they are lying down, you can raise their legs instead.
Did they faint and are they still not responding?
Stay with them and talk to them. Watch whether they respond and how they breathe. Give water if they are awake and can swallow, and ask what might have caused it (hunger, heat, standing for long).
Let them get up slowly, only when they feel better: they may feel faint again.

do_not: Do not let them stand up quickly.
notes: A faint should last only seconds. If they do not wake up at once, it may be something more serious, such as a heart problem: call {number}.
If they fell, check for a head injury.

guides.chat_now: Let them rest in light clothes and drink plenty of fluids. You can sponge them with lukewarm (not cold) water. Call {number} if the fever comes with a rash, confusion or a change in behaviour, trouble breathing, severe belly pain, or eyes hurting in the light with vomiting.
guides.title: Fever (high temperature)
guides.when: Temperature 38°C (100.4°F) or more, hot and sweaty, or shivering.

steps.text: Help them rest and dress lightly. Do not cover them with heavy blankets.
Give water or other fluids to drink often, to replace what they lose by sweating.
You can sponge them with lukewarm water if they like it. Never use cold water.

If they feel really unwell, a fever medicine such as paracetamol can help: give only the dose written on the label or the prescription. Ask a doctor or pharmacist first for older people, or anyone with liver problems or on other medicines.
steps.log: Fever medicine as on the label

steps.text: Call {number} now if the fever comes with a rash, a change in how they think or behave (confused, very sleepy), trouble breathing, severe belly pain, eyes hurting in the light with vomiting, or cold, pale and clammy skin.
See a doctor soon if they are over 65, have cancer or a weak immune system, if the fever lasts more than 3 days or does not come down with the medicine, or if anything else worries you.

do_not: Do not use cold water or ice: it makes the body keep its heat in and causes shivering.
Do not wrap them in thick blankets or many layers.
notes: A fever is a temperature above 38°C (100.4°F). Above 39°C (102.5°F) it can be harmful.
Where malaria is common, see a doctor for any fever, even without other signs.
